title: SSRIs target prefrontal to raphe circuits during development modulating synaptic connectivity and emotional behavior.
ehr_evidence: The study used mice (C57BL/6 and transgenic SERT-Cre, SERT fl/fl, Emx1bCre, Pet1Cre, Ai14 reporter lines) and ex vivo brain tissue; no electronic/computerised health records were used.
summary: A preclinical experimental mouse study examining how developmental exposure to the SSRI fluoxetine and genetic SERT loss-of-function alter PFC-to-dorsal raphe nucleus (DRN) synaptic wiring and adult emotional/stress-coping behavior.
key_findings: SERT-KO mice showed a 40% increase in VGLUT1+ cortical axon boutons in the DRN (F1,6 = 36.45, p < 0.001), with VGLUT2+ and GAD2+ inputs unchanged (F1,6 = 0.24, p = 0.64; F1,6 = 0.34, p = 0.58).
Postnatal fluoxetine (P2–P14, 10 mg/kg/day) reproduced this effect with a 47% increase in VGLUT1+ cortical synaptic innervations in the DRN (F1,8 = 9.94, p < 0.02).
PFC-SERT+ neurons provided the majority of cortical inputs to the DRN, with 67 ± 8.0% of VGLUT1+/synapsin+ terminals colabeled with TdTomato.

Cortex-specific SERT ablation (SERT-KOCTX) increased VGLUT1+ synaptic boutons by 30% (Welch's statistic = 11.20, p < 0.03), whereas raphe-specific ablation (SERT-KORaphe) produced no change (F1,5 = 3.76, p = 0.11).
SERT-KO mice showed larger optogenetically evoked AMPAR-EPSCs in the DRN (genotype main effect F1,29 = 9.32, p < 0.01) with no change in AMPAR/NMDAR ratios (F1,30 = 0.16, p = 0.69).

Early-life fluoxetine increased FST immobility (treatment main effect F1,44 = 5.228, p < 0.03) and NSF feeding latency (F3,40 = 6.994, p < 0.001); chemogenetic activation of PFC-SERT+ neurons rescued these deficits while inhibition enhanced them.
VGLUT2+ and GAD2+ synaptic inputs onto 5-HT neurons were unaffected by SERT loss-of-function (no significant changes).
study_design: Experimental preclinical animal study (genetic and pharmacological manipulation in mice)
population: Mice (C57BL/6 and transgenic lines) from postnatal (P2) to adulthood (P80+)
exposure_domain: SSRIs (fluoxetine) and genetic SERT loss-of-function (serotonin transporter, Slc6a4)
limitations: Mouse model limits human translational relevance.
Synaptic changes observed in juvenile animals; persistence into adult life undetermined.
